strengths: Principled bridge between classical phylogenetic CTMCs and expressive protein language models: COSINE conditions per-site rate matrices on the full sequence context, retaining tractable factorized likelihoods while capturing epistatic effects. This is a clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution.

The theoretical framing is careful and honest: Proposition 4.1 gives an O((λt)^2) L1 error bound via a clean uniformization argument (Appendix D.1), Lemma 4.2 establishes exactness of Gillespie sampling under stated conditions, and the authors explicitly acknowledge the training-time bias that arises when the rate-matching assumption is violated, studying it empirically (Appendix C.1-C.3) rather than hiding it.

Strong empirical validation of the theory: synthetic codon experiments show error scaling and Gillespie superiority over matrix exponentiation as epistasis increases (Figures S2-S3), and real-data experiments show Gillespie better preserves evolutionary distances (Figure S4).

The selection score (log-likelihood ratio against a frozen SHM model, Eq. 5) is a mathematically consistent alternative to DASM's clamped selection factors, and Figure S6 gives an intuitive, convincing analysis of how the SHM correction removes nucleotide-edit-distance bias in VEP.

Comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility: full training details, dataset processing pipeline, pseudocode for all three algorithms, baseline evaluation protocols, and multiple ablations (paired vs. single-chain conditioning, TAG vs. exact guidance with 500-900x speedup verification).

The Guided Gillespie/TAG construction (Eqs. 6-9) is an elegant adaptation of classifier guidance for CTMCs over sequential point mutation processes, with a practical Taylor approximation that provably avoids training the predictor on noisy sequences.
Limitations are candidly discussed (first-order misspecification, no indels, failed SNR-weighting on real data), and the impact statement is appropriate.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is narrow: zero-shot VEP is limited to four DMS assays from FLAb2, two of which (Shaneh.) contain only ~200 sequences. Differences of 0.03-0.06 Spearman over DASM in Table 1 are not accompanied by statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or seed variance, and in the Pearson-correlation version (Table S3) DASM actually matches or exceeds COSINE on two of seven datasets, weakening the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

The guided generation and CDR optimization experiments (Sections 5.4-5.5) are evaluated with the same oracle predictors used for guidance (Jin et al. RNN neutralization scores), creating circularity: fitness gains show the sampler optimizes the oracle, not that actual binding improves. No experimental or orthogonal computational validation of generated binders is provided. The CDR optimization comparison (Table S4) shows COSINE's mean ΔBind (0.198) is essentially identical to the genetic algorithm (0.196), so the claimed advantage is marginal.

The branch length t = 0.2 for all VEP experiments is a fixed, seemingly arbitrary hyperparameter with no sensitivity analysis, even though the selection score and its approximation quality depend on t.

The claim in the conclusion of being 'the first to draw an explicit connection between discrete diffusion and classical sequence evolution models' is overstated; the guidance machinery is directly adapted from Nisonoff et al. (2025), and the connection between CTMC generators and discrete diffusion/flow generators is implicit in that cited work.

The theory relies on the exact rate-matching assumption (Qθ(x)ℓ)xℓ,yℓ = Qx,y, which training does not enforce; the authors' proposed remedy (SNR weighting) failed on the real antibody dataset, so the practical model operates outside the regime where the O(t²) bound rigorously applies. The mitigation is empirical rather than principled.

Model-fit comparison (Section 5.1) reports perplexity for only the heavy chain on one dataset (Rodriguez et al.), and the head-to-head with DASM+Thrifty (62.3% of transitions) is presented without significance testing.

Guided affinity maturation experiments primarily use a single clonal tree (13 leaves, ~60 samples per condition); while Figure S8 extends to more seeds, the sample sizes remain small and only the SARS-CoV-1/2 setting is explored.

No comparison against the strong SiteRM baseline (Prillo et al., 2024), which the paper itself highlights as beating protein LMs on ProteinGym; broader benchmarking (e.g., ProteinGym) is absent, limiting assessment of generalization beyond antibodies.

strengths: The core idea is well motivated and clearly articulated: combining the temporal grounding of phylogenetic CTMCs with the expressivity of neural rate parameterization to model antibody affinity maturation, rather than treating clonal sequences as i.i.d. samples.

The paper provides genuine theoretical grounding: Proposition 4.1 gives an error bound for the factorized approximation of a sequential point mutation process via a clean uniformization argument, and Lemma 4.2 establishes exactness of the Gillespie procedure under stated conditions.

The authors are unusually transparent about the gap between theory and practice: Section C.1 explicitly acknowledges that training with the factorized objective (Eq. 2) violates the assumption of Proposition 4.1, and they run synthetic codon experiments (Sections B.1, C.2) that empirically validate the O(t²) scaling and the advantage of Gillespie sampling, plus a real-data validation (Section C.3).
The selection score disentangling SHM from selection (Eq. 5, Figure S6) is a sensible and interpretable contribution, with an intuitive analysis showing removal of edit-distance bias.

The appendix is thorough, including honest negative results (SNR weighting did not help on real data), ablations on paired vs. single-chain conditioning, and a TAG-vs-exact-guidance comparison with large speedups.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is undermined by the training procedure. Proposition 4.1 requires (Qθ(x)ℓ)xℓ,yℓ = Qx,y, i.e., that the learned per-site matrices recover instantaneous rates of the true process. The authors concede that MLE under the factorized likelihood learns 'effective rates' that absorb unobserved epistatic intermediates, so the assumption fails for the trained model. Their proposed remedy (SNR weighting) helped in the synthetic setting but yielded no improvement on the real antibody data (Section C.1). As a result, both the error bound and Lemma 4.2 apply only to a model they cannot actually train, and the theoretical contribution is largely motivational rather than a guarantee about the deployed system.

The practical relevance of the O(t²) bound is questionable. The footnote in D.1 notes that λ (the maximum exit rate of the sequence-level generator) scales linearly with sequence length. With t calibrated to expected mutations per site, λt for a ~110–220 residue antibody is far from small, making the (λt)² bound effectively vacuous at realistic branch lengths; the intuition that 'O(λt) dominates O(λ²t²)' does not hold at the sequence level.

The VEP evaluation is narrow and the gains are marginal. Results are reported on only four DMS assays (seven datasets) from a single benchmark family (FLAb2), several of which are tiny (Shaneh. datasets have 184 and 201 sequences). Improvements over DASM are small (e.g., 0.613 vs 0.596, 0.498 vs 0.450, and an exact tie at 0.536), no statistical significance tests are reported, and under Pearson correlation (Table S3) DASM actually marginally outperforms COSINE on Koenig (H) (0.688 vs 0.687). Claims of 'state-of-the-art' VEP rest on very limited evidence, and stronger classical baselines such as SiteRM (Prillo et al., 2024) on ProteinGym are cited but not compared.

The guidance and optimization experiments are circular and weakly evaluated. Guided Gillespie is evaluated using the same RNN oracle (Jin et al., 2021) that steers sampling, so 'affinity gain' (Figure 5) may simply reflect exploitation of the predictor rather than real binding improvement; γ ≥ 10 exceeding known binders confirms oracle exploitation is occurring. The affinity maturation experiment samples leaves of a single 13-leaf clonal tree repeated 5 times (~62 samples), a very small evaluation. In the CDR optimization task (Table S4), COSINE's mean fitness gain (0.198) is essentially indistinguishable from a simple genetic algorithm (0.196), and the PoE baselines achieve comparable max gains, so the claimed advantage in Section 5.5 is not clearly supported.

The inter-chain epistasis story is internally inconsistent. Section 5.2 presents the categorical Jacobian as evidence of biologically meaningful intra- and inter-chain coupling, and Section 5.3 claims inter-chain interactions are important, but Table S2 shows single-chain conditioning outperforms paired conditioning on four of seven datasets, and the authors admit this 'could be an artifact of training data composition.' The qualitative Figure 3 analysis (one antibody, no ground truth) does not compensate for this.

Novelty of the guidance component is overstated. The conclusion claims to be 'the first to draw an explicit connection between discrete diffusion and classical sequence evolution models,' yet Section 4.2 states that Guided Gillespie 'follows from Nisonoff et al.' (2025); the contribution amounts to applying an existing CTMC guidance result to a different rate parameterization with a Taylor approximation. This is a useful engineering step, not a new conceptual connection.

The selection score depends on reconstructed wildtype nucleotide sequences (IMGT mapping plus backtranslation to the highest-frequency codon, Section B.3.1), and sensitivity of VEP results to these reconstruction choices is not analyzed. The fixed branch length t = 0.2 for all VEP experiments is also presented without a sensitivity analysis.

No code or model release is mentioned, which, combined with a multi-stage pipeline (partis clustering, IQ-TREE ASR, Thrifty likelihoods, backtranslation), limits reproducibility of the headline results.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: language models treat antibody sequences as i.i.d. samples while classical phylogenetic models lack expressivity. COSINE's conditional site-independent parameterization (Eq. 2) is a clean and natural way to bridge the two paradigms.

The theoretical contribution is careful and non-trivial: the uniformization-based proof that the factorized model is a first-order approximation of the sequential point-mutation CTMC with O(t^2) error (Prop. 4.1), and the exactness lemma for Gillespie sampling (Lemma 4.2), are correct as presented and give the empirical claims real grounding.

The authors are commendably honest about the gap between theory and practice: they acknowledge that training with the factorized objective does not enforce the instantaneous-rate assumption, and they empirically quantify the quadratic-in-branch-length error in both synthetic (Sec. C.2, Fig. S3) and real-data settings (Sec. C.3, Fig. S4), which strongly supports the theory.

Empirical evaluation is broad and multi-pronged: (i) head-to-head likelihood comparison against DASM+Thrifty on ~2M held-out transitions with improvement concentrated at long branch lengths as predicted; (ii) SOTA zero-shot VEP on FLAb2 against strong baselines (DASM, ESM-2, ProGen2, AbLang-2); (iii) ablations isolating the selection-score correction (Fig. 4, Fig. S6) and inter-chain effects (Table S2); (iv) synthetic codon experiments validating Props. 4.1/4.2; (v) guidance ablations (exact vs. Taylor guidance, 500-900x speedup with no significant fitness difference).

The Guided Gillespie / TAG guidance is a well-derived and practical contribution: building on Nisonoff et al.'s posterior transition density, the adaptive threshold r0 = mu(x) and Taylor-linearized guidance make it tractable, and the generated sequences are checked for structural plausibility (pLDDT) and humanness (OASis), not just oracle scores.

Reproducibility appears strong: full training hyperparameters, data sources and splits matched to prior work, algorithm pseudocode for all samplers, and detailed descriptions of the DMS protocols and baselines.
weaknesses: The VEP evidence base is narrow: only four DMS assays from a single benchmark (FLAb2), some with very few sequences (Shaneh. 119/120 have 184/201 samples). Several Spearman gaps over DASM are small (e.g., Shaneh. 120 is a tie at 0.536; Koenig L within 0.005 of ProGen2-Small), and Table 1 reports no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests. Broader coverage (e.g., ProteinGym antibody subsets) would materially strengthen the SOTA claim.

The theory-practice gap deserves more emphasis: Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 hinge on (Qθ(x)ℓ)_{xℓ,yℓ} = Q_{x,y}, but the training objective does not enforce this, and the proposed remedy (SNR weighting) failed to help on real data (Sec. C.1). The bounds are therefore stated under an assumption the deployed model only approximately satisfies; the paper handles this empirically but the framing sometimes overstates the theoretical guarantee.

Guided design results are validated only in silico with RNN oracles trained on CoV-AbDab. The γ≥10 regime producing scores above real binders confirms oracle exploitation is a real risk here, and there is no wet-lab or structural-binding validation that guided samples actually bind.

Confounding in the baseline comparison: COSINE is initialized from ESM2-150M, yet ESM2-150M is one of the weaker VEP baselines. No ablation of the backbone (e.g., random initialization or a different PLM) is provided, so the relative contribution of the pretrained backbone vs. the evolutionary formulation is not fully disentangled.

The upstream pipeline introduces unexamined dependencies: branch lengths and parent-child pairs come from ancestral sequence reconstruction with IQ-TREE under a DNA K80 model; ASR and tree-inference errors propagate into training targets and the t-calibration, but no sensitivity analysis of this is offered.
The fixed t = 0.2 for all VEP evaluations is a hyperparameter whose sensitivity is not reported, despite the theory predicting strong t-dependence of the approximation error.

Novelty positioning is close to concurrent work (Albors et al., 2025, phylogenetic genomic LM; DASM, Matsen IV et al., 2025). The delta is real—conditional per-transition site-wise rate matrices, the approximation bound, and guidance—but the paper would benefit from more explicit delineation of what is new relative to these.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: COSINE bridges classical phylogenetic CTMCs and deep protein language models by learning context-conditioned, site-specific rate matrices, giving a tractable factorized transition likelihood that captures epistatic effects while retaining explicit temporal/evolutionary grounding.

Solid theoretical foundation: Proposition 4.1 provides an L1 error bound (quadratic in branch length) between the factorized model and the sequential point-mutation process via a clean uniformization argument, and Lemma 4.2 establishes exactness of the Gillespie sampling procedure under stated conditions. The synthetic codon experiments (Sections B.1, C.2) empirically validate both results, showing KL divergence scaling as predicted and that Gillespie sampling recovers the correct stationary distribution.

Strong empirical results: COSINE achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot VEP performance across 7 FLAb2 assays plus 2 additional Petersen assays (Tables 1, S4, S6), fits held-out transitions better than DASM+Thrifty in 62.3% of cases (with larger gains on longer branches), and outperforms WAG/LG+G4 baselines including on general protein families (TrRosetta, Table S3), demonstrating the approach is not antibody-specific.

Thoughtful disentangling of selection from SHM: the log-likelihood-ratio selection score (Eq. 5) is principled (Halpern-Bruno / Kimura framing with proof in D.3), and Figure S6 convincingly shows the correction removes nucleotide edit-distance bias that would otherwise corrupt fitness inference.

Thorough ablations and robustness checks: sensitivity to branch length t (Figure S7), ESM2 backbone ablation showing the evolutionary objective rather than pretraining drives performance (Table S8), paired vs. single-chain conditioning, SNR-weighted loss investigation with honest reporting that it did not help in the real-data setting, and 500-900x speedup of Taylor-approximated guidance with no fitness loss.

Good reproducibility: code and data promised for release, training details (Appendix A), oracle/evaluator details (Appendix B), pseudocode for all three algorithms, and theoretical proofs in Appendix D are all provided.

Honest and substantive limitations section (first-order model misspecification, no indels) and explicit discussion of the rate-bias induced by marginalizing intermediate states on long branches, with follow-up analysis (C.1-C.3).
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees (Prop 4.1, Lemma 4.2) hold only under the assumption that the learned per-site rates match the instantaneous rates of the true generator Q; the model trained via the factorized objective (Eq. 2) does not satisfy this condition, so the guarantees are about an idealized version of the method rather than the deployed model. The authors acknowledge this, but the headline 'provably' framing in the abstract slightly overstates what is guaranteed in practice.

VEP evaluation is confined to a small number of DMS assays, several with modest sample sizes (e.g., Shaneh. n=184/201), and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the Spearman correlations in Table 1; gains over DASM on some datasets (e.g., Koenig Expression L, Shaneh. 120) are within plausible noise ranges.

The epistatic-capture evidence beyond the first-order rate matrix is mostly qualitative: the categorical Jacobian analysis (Figure 3) is a single example sequence with a biologically plausible interpretation, but no quantitative validation that off-diagonal structure improves downstream tasks is provided (the paired-vs-single-chain ablation in Table S5 actually shows single-chain conditioning wins on 4/7 datasets, which the authors explain only speculatively).

Guided sampling and CDR optimization experiments are evaluated entirely in silico against an RNN neutralization oracle (Jin et al. 2022) with MC-dropout uncertainty; no wet-lab or independent validation of generated antibodies is provided, and oracle exploitation under strong guidance (noted at gamma >= 10) leaves open questions about gamma=5 results.

The selection score requires reconstructing the wildtype nucleotide/codon sequence via IMGT germline mapping and backtranslation heuristics (B.3.1), adding an extra layer of assumptions and preprocessing that complicates fair comparison with baselines operating purely on amino acid space.

Some significance questions: the improvement over DASM (the closest baseline, which also disentangles SHM from selection) is real but incremental on several datasets, and the practical value of the Gillespie machinery over the simpler factorized likelihood for VEP is not directly demonstrated.

Minor presentation issues: some citations appear with future dates (e.g., Kim et al. 2026, Koehl et al. 2026, Matsen et al. 2026) that reviewers cannot verify, and the uniformization proof relies on the equality of maximum exit rates across Q and Q_theta(x) which deserves a short justification.

strengths: The paper is technically careful and largely honest about the gap between its theory and practice: Section 4 correctly notes that the training objective (Equation 2) induces bias in the estimated rates relative to the exact instantaneous rates required by Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 4.2, and Sections C.1–C.3 empirically quantify this bias in both synthetic codon and real antibody settings.

The theoretical analysis (uniformization-based proof of the O(t²) error bound in Appendix D.1) is clean and correct, and the synthetic codon experiments (B.1, Figures S2–S3) provide a controlled validation of both the approximation and the Gillespie sampling procedure.

The VEP evaluation is reasonably thorough for its scope: seven FLAb2 assays plus two external Petersen assays, sensible baselines (DASM, PRISM, AbLang-2, ProGen2, ESM-2), a fixed branch length t=0.2 across all assays to avoid test-set tuning, and useful ablations (ESM2 backbone, branch-length sensitivity, paired vs. single-chain context, WAG-style baseline).

The SHM-correction analysis in Section C.7 (Figure S6) convincingly demonstrates that the selection score removes a nucleotide edit-distance bias that would otherwise contaminate fitness correlations — this is a genuinely useful diagnostic contribution.

The limitations section is candid (first-order misspecification, no indels, generalization beyond antibodies), and the training/sampling details in Appendices A–B are detailed enough to support reproduction.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical claims are conditional on an assumption that the authors' own training procedure violates. Proposition 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 require (Qθ(x)ℓ)xℓ,yℓ = Qx,y exactly, but the model is trained with the factorized likelihood, which by their own admission learns 'effective rates' that absorb unobserved intermediate states (Section C.1). Thus 'provably samples from P(·|x,t)' is only true for a model they do not actually train, and the SNR-weighted remedy proposed to fix this failed to help on real data (Section C.1). The practical value of the theory is therefore limited to short branches, where the model is close to a well-fit conditional factorization anyway.

The generative design contribution is evaluated only against in silico oracles, making it circular. Guided affinity maturation (Section 5.4) and CDR optimization (Section 5.5) both use the RefineGNN neutralization predictor as both the guidance signal and the evaluation metric; sequences steered toward higher predicted affinity will trivially score better on the same predictor. The observation that γ ≥ 10 'exploits oracle uncertainty' is itself evidence of this. No wet-lab or even independent-oracle validation is provided, so claims about 'optimization of antibody binding affinity' are unsupported beyond the oracle.

The Table 2 CDR-optimization result is not a meaningful improvement: COSINE's ΔBind_mean (0.198) beats the genetic algorithm (0.196) by 0.002 and ΔBind_max by 0.005, while consuming a comparable oracle budget (5.00 vs. 4.81). Given the circular oracle and this margin, the constrained-optimization experiment does not clearly demonstrate an advantage over simple baselines.

The VEP benchmarks are small and narrow: the Shaneh. datasets contain only 184 and 201 sequences, and all but one assay come from a single benchmark (FLAb2). Spearman correlations on ~200 points have wide confidence intervals, and margins over DASM (the most relevant baseline) are modest on several datasets (e.g., 0.508 vs. 0.474; 0.371 vs. 0.327). A broader ProteinGym-style evaluation would be needed to support the 'state-of-the-art' framing.

Novelty is incremental relative to concurrent/adjacent work the paper itself cites: context-conditioned neural substitution models already exist (Albors et al., 2025; SiteRM, Prillo et al., 2024; Koehl et al., 2026), and the guided-sampling machinery is directly adopted from Nisonoff et al. (2025) with a Taylor approximation for speed. The claim of being 'the first to draw an explicit connection between discrete diffusion and classical sequence evolution models' (Section 6) overstates the contribution, since the connection is imported from that prior work.

There is an unexplained methodological oddity in the phylogenetic pipeline: ancestral sequence reconstruction and tree inference are performed with IQ-TREE under the K80 model, which is a nucleotide substitution model, yet the data appear to be amino-acid sequences (Appendix A.1). It is unclear how K80 was applied, and no sensitivity analysis to ASR/tree-inference error is provided despite the training labels being entirely products of this pipeline.

The reproducibility statement contains a blank code URL ('made publicly available at , including any datasets'), so the promised code release is not verifiable at submission time; several baselines also required bespoke evaluation choices (germline vs. non-germline scoring modes for PRISM, specific repository commits for FLAb2) whose robustness is not analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting gap between classical phylogenetic CTMC models and expressive protein language models, and the COSINE formulation (context-conditioned per-site rate matrices) is a clean and principled way to capture epistasis while retaining tractable likelihoods.

The theoretical results are carefully stated and proved: the uniformization-based proof of the O((λt)²) error bound (Proposition 4.1 / Appendix D.1) is correct and elegant, and the exactness of Gillespie sampling under rate-matching (Lemma 4.2) is properly established.

The theoretical claims are not left unvalidated: the synthetic codon experiments (Sections B.1, C.1, C.2) directly test the quadratic error scaling and the superiority of Gillespie sampling over matrix exponentiation across epistasis levels, and a real-antibody analog (C.3) corroborates the findings.

The empirical evaluation is comparatively thorough: head-to-head comparison with DASM+Thrifty, a WAG-style context-independent baseline, and six PLM baselines on multiple DMS assays (Tables 1, S4, S6), plus useful ablations (ESM2 backbone from-scratch training in C.10, branch-length sensitivity in C.9, paired vs. single-chain conditioning in C.8).

The guided sampling contribution is practically significant: the Taylor-approximated guidance (TAG) achieves ~500-900x speedup over exact guidance with no significant fitness loss (C.11), and runtime scaling is characterized (C.12).

Limitations are discussed honestly (first-order approximation misspecification, no indels), and the paper provides a reproducibility statement with public code, datasets, and detailed training/sampling pseudocode.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee is conditional on exact matching of instantaneous rates, (Qθ(x)ℓ)xℓ,yℓ = Qx,y, but the training objective does not enforce this; the authors acknowledge this bias and their attempted fix (SNR weighting) failed to help on real data (C.1), so the practical gap between theory and the deployed model remains unresolved.

The 'captures epistatic effects' framing is somewhat qualified: the transition likelihood remains fully factorized across sites, so epistasis enters only through state-conditioning of per-site rates; the improvement over DASM in Table 1 is modest on some datasets (e.g., +0.005 on Koenig Expression L), and the evaluation covers only ~9 antibody DMS assays, some with very few sequences (Shaneh. n≈184-201), rather than a broad benchmark like ProteinGym.

The zero-shot VEP comparison uses different scoring mechanisms for COSINE (selection score with Thrifty correction) versus baselines (pseudo-perplexity/perplexity), and the selection score requires heuristic reconstruction of wildtype nucleotide sequences via backtranslation; these methodological asymmetries are described but their confounding effect is not fully quantified.

The design applications (Sections 5.4, 5.5) are validated entirely in silico against an RNN oracle trained on CoV-AbDab; the observation that γ ≥ 10 'produced scores exceeding biological binders (likely exploiting oracle uncertainty)' is a red flag that guidance may exploit oracle pathologies, and no wet-lab or orthogonal experimental validation of the generated antibodies is provided.

The claim of being 'the first to draw an explicit connection between discrete diffusion and classical sequence evolution models' overstates novelty: the guidance machinery is directly adopted from Nisonoff et al. (2025), and context-conditioned neural substitution models already exist (e.g., Albors et al., 2025; SiteRM), so the conceptual novelty is incremental even if the antibody-specific instantiation is new.

The Gillespie sampling superiority on real trees (C.3) rests on proxy metrics (Hamming distance to held-out leaves) under a stated assumption, and the margin (52.0% vs 38.8%) is not accompanied by significance testing.
